inclusion_criteria: Primary sources (peer-reviewed papers or arXiv preprints) that present methods, experiments, tools, datasets, or benchmarks relevant to LLMs/agents for NetOps.
Tool papers and documentation for network-verification frameworks (e.g., Batfish, Veriflow, NetKAT, Header Space Analysis) including reproducible artifacts.
Benchmark descriptions and publicly available datasets or code repositories (6G-Bench, TSNBench, OpsEval, RIPE/RouteViews/CAIDA) where accessible.
Works proposing or evaluating mitigations, validators, formal methods, staged deployment strategies, or human-in-the-loop designs for automated NetOps.
Research from neighboring domains (IaC, program synthesis, AIOps, automated debugging) that provide transferable methods or evaluation frameworks.
Studies that include quantitative evaluation, failure analysis, or reproducibility artifacts, or that clearly describe evaluation metrics and limitations.
Publicly accessible software, datasets, or experiment descriptions enabling independent verification or reproduction where possible.
exclusion_criteria: Vendor marketing materials, product one-pagers, or promotional blog posts lacking primary experimental evidence or method detail (unless they link to primary artifacts).
Opinion pieces or editorials without empirical or technical content directly supporting methodological claims.
Non-English sources unless they provide unique primary results and can be verified/translated reliably.
Proprietary datasets, closed-source tools, or private preprints that are inaccessible and cannot be independently verified.
Works unrelated to network operations (purely general NLP benchmarks with no NetOps transfer or evaluation).
Any pre-lock internal development artifacts from the programme (per autonomy constraints).
date_rationale: Cover classical and foundational network-verification and configuration synthesis literature (approx. 2005 onward) while prioritizing recent advances relevant to LLMs and agentic systems (2018–2026). Rationale: network-verification and synthesis have older foundational work vital for validators, whereas LLM-driven methods, agent frameworks, hallucination/verification research, and benchmarks have accelerated since 2020–2023; include up-to-date preprints through 2026 to capture the latest agentic/LLM-for-AIOps work.
